title: Tobin and the Stormy Day
markdown:
Gadzooks, but the Saltwind Market Square — usually alive with vendors’ shouts and the scent of sea-kissed bread — buzzed with nervous energy. It was Judging Day, and for Tobin, a shaggy goat whose beard rivalled his anxiety, it was everything. He smoothed his wool, his mind on lighthouse duties. Helping at the lighthouse, he felt, was the most important job in Port Blossom.

His mother’s voice, a comforting rustle of hay, echoed from earlier that morning. “Inspectors love confidence, Tobin. Stand tall, look them in the eye.” Tobin had nodded so hard his tiny bell had gone berserk. He aimed for calm competence, especially for Inspector Primrose.

Beside him, Felix the stoat meticulously polished a brass barometer. Felix, Tobin’s lab partner, spoke only when necessary — a trait Tobin found maddening.

“The air feels heavy,” Felix murmured, his whiskers twitching as he watched the needle. “A change is coming.”

Tobin snorted, a puff of mist. “Don’t be silly, Felix. Clear skies predicted. Inspector Primrose won’t be impressed by phantom storms.” He adjusted his lighthouse keeper’s hat, his hooves gleaming from a recent buff. Polishing was surprisingly tiring.

Inspector Primrose arrived then, her sharp eyes missing nothing. She paused, fixing her gaze on Tobin. “Lighthouse helper,” she announced, her voice cutting through the chatter. “Report.”

Tobin puffed his chest, channeling his mother. “All in order, Inspector. Lamp clean, oil full, foghorn tested. Perfectly prepared.” He attempted a confident wink, which felt more like a facial spasm.

Felix, however, stared at the horizon, his brow furrowed. The sky had turned a bruised purple. He nudged Tobin. “Tobin, reconsider. The wind’s picking up. Gulls are flying inland.”

“Quiet, Felix!” Tobin hissed, eyes on the Inspector. “She wants efficiency, not panic!”

Inspector Primrose’s eyebrow rose. “An issue, helper?”

Tobin forced a wide smile. “Not at all, Inspector. Just optimising presentation.” He gestured vaguely at the sky, as if controlling its mood.

A violent gust tore through the square, snatching awnings and sending lanterns spiraling. Then fat splatters of rain hammered the cobblestones.

“It appears,” Inspector Primrose stated, her voice steady, “the elements are prematurely curtailing my inspection.”

Tobin’s calm shattered. “But the forecast…” he stammered, hooves clattering. He looked utterly out of his depth.

Felix was a blur of motion. He scrambled for a heavy oilskin tarp, expertly securing it over crates. “This way, Inspector! The main shed is dry. We can move valuable supplies. And Tobin — the emergency flares are in the third locker. Keep them dry.”

Tobin stared, dumbfounded, as the Inspector’s gaze shifted from his floundering to Felix’s efficiency. The stoat wasn’t performing. He was doing.

For a moment the square held its breath — rain on stone, the distant lighthouse beam still faithful, paper lanterns tugging at their strings. Inspector Primrose, her stern face softening, followed Felix. She watched him calmly direct bewildered townspeople to shelter. Reaching the shed, she turned to the stoat. “Your advice on the weather. You saw this coming, didn’t you?”

Felix nodded, water cascading from his whiskers. “The signs were clear, Inspector. True preparedness is more than a clean lamp. It’s anticipating the sea. It’s foresight.”

Tobin, dripping and sheepish, understood. His confident act had been a flimsy shield. Felix, the quiet stoat, had been the true helper — foresight and action far more valuable than any boast.

Later, as the squall subsided and a hesitant moon peeked through the clouds, the market square lay in disarray, yet strangely beautiful. Paper lanterns, miraculously intact, bobbed, casting shimmering reflections.

Inspector Primrose approached Tobin. “Helper,” she began, and Tobin braced for a lecture. Instead a small smile touched her lips. “Your zeal is commendable, Tobin. But true leadership comes not from appearing calm, but from being prepared and listening to those who see the truth.” She turned to Felix, her voice warming. “And you, my dear stoat, have exceptional foresight. Commendations for your quick thinking.”

Tobin watched, a lump in his throat, as Felix accepted the nod with quiet dignity. Warmth spread through him — understanding, humility, and respect. He nudged Felix. “You were right, Felix. About everything.”

Felix’s dark eyes met Tobin’s. “We make a good team, Tobin. Even if my pronouncements are sometimes subtle.”

Tobin chuckled, a sound more genuine than forced bravado. “Maybe my job is to make the big noises. And your job is to make sure those noises are for the right reasons.” He glanced from the safe goods to the lighthouse beam, which had never needed a wink to stay lit — and if you listen on the next Judging Day, you may still hear a goat’s bell and a stoat’s barometer agreeing, very softly, about the weather.
characters: Tobin (a goat lighthouse helper), Felix (a stoat lab partner)
